q: 1. A 1st class brick immersed in water for 24 hours, should not absorb water (by weight) more than
explain: First class bricks must not absorb more than about 15% of their weight in water after 24-hour immersion.

q: 2. A pug mill is used for
explain: A pug mill kneads and tempers clay to a uniform, workable consistency free of air pockets before molding.

q: 3. The soil used for the manufacture of bricks should preferably not contain the following material
explain: Alkalies, pebbles, and kankar all cause defects (efflorescence, weak spots, unsoundness) and should be avoided in brick earth.

q: 4. The nature of refractories material is
explain: Refractory materials are designed to withstand high temperatures and often require low porosity to resist chemical attack.

q: 5. The ingredient of the brick earth which enables the brick to retain shape is
explain: Silica prevents the brick from warping, shrinking, and cracking; it provides the 'skeleton' for shape retention.

q: 6. The red colour of the brick is due to
explain: Iron oxide (roughly 5-6%) acts as a flux and imparts the characteristic red color to the brick upon burning.

q: 7. For what purpose are fire bricks used
options: to protect the building against lightening
explain: Fire bricks are used to line furnaces/kilns, insulating structures by decreasing heat flow while withstanding high temperatures.

q: 8. Excess of alumina in a brick earth causes
explain: Excess alumina makes the clay too plastic, leading to significant shrinkage, cracking, and warping during the drying and burning process.

q: 9. Lime is mixed with brick earth
explain: Lime in brick earth helps the silica to fuse at a lower temperature and prevents the raw bricks from shrinking and warping.

q: 10. The soil used for the manufacture of bricks should preferably not contain the following material
explain: Pebbles and stones prevent the uniform mixing of clay and can cause the brick to crack during the burning process.

q: 11. Advantage of clamp burning as compared to kiln burning is
options: when large number of bricks are required
explain: Clamps are temporary structures and do not require the expensive permanent construction associated with kilns.

q: 12. The over ground continuous kiln is
explain: Hoffman's kiln is a permanent, over-ground continuous kiln, whereas Bull's Trench is typically partially underground.

q: 13. Excess of silica in brick earth causes
explain: Excess silica reduces the clay's plasticity and binding capacity, causing loss of cohesion and brittle, weak bricks.

q: 14. Hoffman's kiln is a
explain: Hoffman's kilns allow for continuous loading, burning, and unloading of bricks in different chambers simultaneously.

q: 15. The bricks used for lining of furnaces is
explain: Refractory (fire) bricks are specifically made to withstand the intense heat inside furnaces and chimneys.

q: 16. Fire bricks should be laid in a
explain: To maintain thermal consistency, fire bricks are laid using fire clay mortar which can resist similar high temperatures.

q: 17. In bricks masonry, the frog of the brick generally kept on
explain: The 'frog' (indentation) is placed facing up so that it can be filled with mortar, creating a mechanical key with the course above.

q: 18. Hollow bricks are used for
explain: The air trapped inside hollow bricks acts as an excellent thermal insulator, keeping interiors cooler in summer and warmer in winter.

q: 19. Bloating of bricks is due to
options: presence of excess carbonaceous matter and sulphur
presence of any gas forming material in clay
explain: Bloating is a spongy swollen mass caused by the entrapped gases from carbonaceous matter and sulphur during firing.

q: 20. Swelling of bricks is known as
explain: Bloating is the term for the permanent swelling of a brick, often caused by internal gas pressure during burning.

q: 21. In one day, the height of brick masonry construction should generally not exceed
explain: To prevent the fresh mortar in lower courses from being crushed by the weight of new work, the daily height is limited to 1m.

q: 22. Frog means
explain: In masonry terminology, a frog is the depression or indentation made on the top face of a brick.

q: 23. Generally wooden moulds are made from
explain: Hardwoods like Shisham are preferred for brick moulds because they resist wear and warping from moisture.

q: 24. Choose the correct statement
options: percentage of silica is increased in 1st class brick
percentage of alumina is increased in refractory brick
percentage of alumina is increased in 1st class brick
explain: Refractory bricks require a higher percentage of alumina (and silica) to withstand extreme temperatures without melting.

q: 25. The discolouration and formation of white deposits due to presence of relatively large proportion of soluble salts in a bricks is known as
explain: Efflorescence is the white powdery deposit left on a brick surface when moisture evaporates and leaves behind soluble salts.

q: 26. The most widely used kiln in Nepal is
explain: Bull's Trench Kiln is the most popular type in Nepal due to its cost-efficiency and ability to produce a large volume of bricks continuously.

q: 27. Advantage of a clamp compared to a kiln for burning bricks is that
options: it takes less time for burning
it gives more output of first class bricks
it is suitable when bricks are required in large numbers
explain: A clamp requires far less capital investment to set up compared to a permanent kiln structure.

q: 28. The thermal conductivity of glass is
explain: Glass has low thermal conductivity, making it a relatively poor conductor of heat.

q: 29. Efflorescence in bricks is caused by
options: the high pH content of water used during pugging
low silica content of the bricks
explain: Efflorescence results from soluble alkaline salts within the brick migrating to the surface and crystallizing as water evaporates.

q: 30. Percentage of silica in a good brick earth lies between
explain: Silica forms the bulk of good brick earth, typically comprising about 50 to 60%.

q: 31. The stretcher bond in brick masonry can be used only when the thickness of wall is
explain: Since stretcher bond shows only the long face of bricks, it is suitable only for half-brick-thick (9 cm) walls.

q: 32. Minimum thickness of wall where single flemish bond can be used is
options: one and a half bricks thick
explain: Single Flemish bond requires a minimum wall thickness of one and a half bricks to properly interlock headers and stretchers.

q: 33. What should be the ratio of water absorption of a first class brick after 24 hours immersion?
explain: First class bricks should have a water absorption not exceeding about 20% of their weight after 24-hour immersion.

q: 34. A small quantity of magnesia in brick earth imparts
explain: A small amount of magnesia in brick earth is known to impart a yellowish tint to the fired brick.
